drip.author: sump_pump_sam
drip.title: Before the fall rain shows up, go pour a bucket of water into your sump pit
drip.body:
It's the one test that matters and almost nobody does it until the basement does it for them. Lid off the pit, pour water in slowly until the float rises, and watch. The pump should kick on, empty the pit, and shut itself off. Keep your hands out of the pit while it's plugged in. Then go outside and check that the water actually came out where it's supposed to, well away from the foundation, and not into a flower bed hugging the wall.

While you're down there: fish out anything that fell into the pit over the summer, make sure the discharge line outside isn't crushed or clogged, and look at your downspouts. Every litre that comes off the roof and lands next to the foundation is a litre your pump gets to deal with twice.

In a 1962 house the sump pump is the most important employee I have. It gets a performance review every September whether it wants one or not.

comments.author: watts_the_damage
comments.body: If you've got a battery backup pump, test that too. Unplug the main pump, pour the bucket, and make sure the backup actually takes over. The batteries in those don't last forever and they die quietly. Then plug the main one back in, which sounds obvious right up until you forget.

replies.author: sump_pump_sam
replies.body: And write the install date on the battery in marker. Future you will not remember what year anything happened. Trust me on that one.

comments.author: borrowed_ladder
comments.body: Didn't know I had a sump pump until tonight. Went looking, found a lid in the basement floor behind the furnace, poured the bucket. It worked. I have never felt more like a person who owns a house.

replies.author: sump_pump_sam
replies.body: Welcome to the job. It needs you once a year, plus one terrible stormy night when you'll be very glad you checked.

comments.author: OttomanEmpire
comments.body: Did it. Pump worked fine, but the end of the discharge hose outside had a mouse nest packed into it. So the pump was pumping and the mice were blocking. Nobody told me I was running a rental property. Anyway, I'm pumped that I checked. I'll see myself out.

drip.author: OttomanEmpire
drip.title: Want to try upholstery? Start with a drop-in dining chair seat, not a wingback.
drip.body:
Everyone wants to start with the big dramatic chair. Don't. Start with a dining chair where the seat is just a board that unscrews from underneath. Four screws, one board, no sewing, and you learn the one skill that actually matters, which is pulling fabric tight without wrinkles.

Take the seat off, strip the old fabric, and replace the foam if it crumbles when you squeeze it. Batting over the foam, then fabric. Put one staple in the centre of each side first, front, back, left, right, pulling each side against its opposite, then work out toward the corners. Corners get folded like you're wrapping a present, and you will redo the first one. Everyone redoes the first one.

The mistake nobody warns you about: when the seat goes back on, use the same screws that came out. Grab a longer one from the jar and you'll find out the next time somebody sits down. Upholstery is all about getting to the point. Just not that point.

comments.author: borrowed_ladder
comments.body: The curb footstool from the summer is finished, by the way. Hand stapler, one evening, and the corners look like I wrapped them in the dark. It's lumpy. I love it. Doing the kitchen chairs next, because apparently that's how this goes.

replies.author: OttomanEmpire
replies.body: Lumpy is just hand-finished. That footstool got rescued from a curb. It doesn't need to be perfect, it needs to be sat on.

comments.author: sump_pump_sam
comments.body: Redid one dining chair years ago and I still tell it like a war story. The screw thing got me too. Lost two of the originals, grabbed replacements from the coffee can, screwed the seat back on feeling like a craftsman. A dinner guest found them for me. Once.

comments.author: thrifted_thunder
comments.body: Bargain hunter tip that pairs perfectly with this: thrift stores are full of solid wood dining chairs going for almost nothing because the seats are stained or tragic. I got a set of four for $20 last month. Ugly seats are basically a discount code.

drip.author: borrowed_ladder
drip.title: Cleaned my gutters for the first time. The ladder was, of course, borrowed.
drip.body:
Neighbour's extension ladder, and twenty whole minutes of reading beforehand, which for me is thorough. The rules I learned just in time: for every four feet of height, the base sits one foot out from the wall. Three points of contact, so one hand scoops and the other hangs on. Stay off the top rungs no matter how close the gutter looks. And move the ladder every few feet instead of leaning out, which is the one I most wanted to break. The neighbour held the bottom, mostly to supervise his ladder.

Found in my gutters: about a wheelbarrow of black sludge, a tennis ball I cannot explain, and a small maple tree roughly thirty centimetres tall that had been living up there independently. Flushed the downspouts with the hose after and one was completely plugged, which explains the waterfall over the front step every time it rains.

Nobody fell. The tree has been relocated to the yard. I'm calling it a full success.

comments.author: watts_the_damage
comments.body: Adding the one that gets people with aluminum ladders: look up before you move it. Know where the power line comes into the house and keep the whole ladder well clear of it, at least a few metres, including while you're walking it around a corner. Aluminum conducts, and it only takes one wobble.

replies.author: borrowed_ladder
replies.body: Did not think about that for one second. The line comes in on the opposite corner, which I am going to describe as planning.

comments.author: sump_pump_sam
comments.body: A plugged downspout plus a waterfall over the step is exactly the kind of water that finds its way into a basement. You just saved your sump pump a bad night. Next weekend: that deck you stained at 2 pm?

replies.author: borrowed_ladder
replies.body: The deck is a spring problem. The deck knows what it did.

comments.author: compost_mentis
comments.body: gardener passing through: that sludge is half-finished compost that's been curing on your roof. gloves on, and I'd put it under shrubs or on a flower bed rather than the vegetables, since it's spent a year on shingles. the gutter maple has an origin story most trees would envy

late_comments.author: borrowed_ladder
late_comments.body: Found this after the shutoff under my bathroom sink wouldn't budge this week. Didn't force it. Shut the main first, the correct valve on the first try, which for me is a personal best, and swapped in a quarter-turn like you said. One hour, zero water on the floor. Growth.
